title: The Isthmus and the Jungle: Relative Clauses

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know relative clauses with *que* and *quien* from B1 Unit 5. They let you add information about a person, a thing or a place inside one sentence. Panama's geography is a good place to use them: an isthmus is a strip of land *que* joins two continents, and the Darién is a jungle *que* has no road.

sections.title: Que and quien at work
rows: El istmo es una franja de tierra que une dos continentes.
*que* for a thing: the isthmus is a strip of land that joins two continents
La selva que está en el este del país no tiene carretera.
*que* for a place: the jungle that lies in the east of the country has no road
Los migrantes que cruzan la selva se enfrentan a muchos peligros.
*que* for people: the migrants who cross the jungle face many dangers
Los guías con quienes hablamos conocen bien el río.
*quien* after a preposition: the guides we talked to know the river well

items.spanish: La Carretera Panamericana, que recorre casi todo el continente, se interrumpe en el Darién.
items.english: The Pan-American Highway, which runs along almost the whole continent, stops in the Darién.

items.spanish: Los emberá, que viven junto a los ríos, conocen bien la selva.
items.english: The Emberá, who live beside the rivers, know the jungle well.

items.spanish: El águila harpía, que es el ave nacional de Panamá, vive en el Darién.
items.english: The harpy eagle, which is Panama's national bird, lives in the Darién.

items.spanish: Las personas con quienes habló el periodista caminaron varios días.
items.english: The people the journalist spoke to walked for several days.

sections.content: *Que* is the usual choice for people, things and places. *Quien* (plural *quienes*) is for people only, and you mostly need it after a preposition: *con quienes*, *de quienes*. A comma before *que* gives extra information (*El Darién, que está en el este, es una selva*); without commas the clause says which one you mean.
